title: Tale of King Omar bin al-Nu'uman

full_text:
In the ancient city of Baghdad, long before the Abbasid dynasty, reigned King Omar bin al-Nu'uman, a sovereign of mighty valor who held dominion over Syria, Iraq, and the Arabian peninsula. He possessed an army of a hundred thousand horsemen, a treasury overflowing with tribute, and two valiant sons: Prince Sharrkan, famed for his mastery of the lance, and Prince Zau al-Makan, renowned for his learning and wisdom.

When the Emperor of Constantinople declared war against the realm, King Omar dispatched Sharrkan at the head of twenty thousand horsemen to defend the northern frontiers. Sharrkan marched into the rugged mountains of Anatolia, where he became separated from his troops in an enchanted valley surrounded by cedar forests.

There, beside a marble hermitage, he encountered Princess Abrizah, the daughter of the King of Greece. Though adversaries by allegiance, both possessed souls of supreme nobility and chivalry. They matched their martial prowess in single combat, wrestling with such grace and skill that neither took advantage of the other. Defeated by her agile wit, Sharrkan was moved by her honor and sought to forge a lasting peace between their nations.

Meanwhile, back in Baghdad, King Omar fell into the snares of courtly intrigue and treacherous advisers who preferred endless warfare to honorable treaties. When the king died, it fell upon the two brothers, Sharrkan and Zau al-Makan, to set aside their differences, unite their armies, and discover that true strength lies not in the slaughter of adversaries, but in establishing a reign of justice, religious tolerance, and peaceful commerce across the Mediterranean world.
moral: Great empires and martial glory are hollow unless governed by wisdom, chivalry, and noble restraint.
